solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unusually stoical, extremely smooth, medieval annotator

indicators.note: doing something unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters are put into a new order
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, here of smooth

explanation.surface: A monk scribbling glosses in the margins is oddly calm and polished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes SH, the outer letters of smooth, which join STOICAL; 'Unusually' rearranges all nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholiast wrote scholia, explanatory notes added to ancient and medieval texts.

clue.text: Displaying frivolity in speech about quartz, for example

indicators.note: something said in speech is heard rather than read, so the word for frivolous is taken by its sound

parts.note: someone displaying frivolity is silly
CA is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: Talking frivolously about quartz, perhaps in a geology lecture gone wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in speech' means the frivolous word counts only as heard, so its spelling changes; 'about' is the Latin circa, not a containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Quartz is crystalline silica, so it is one example of the mineral compound.

clue.text: Memorable moments familiar to hairstylists?

definitions.meaning: the ... of an event are its best, most memorable parts
hairstylists dye streaks of hair lighter

explanation.surface: Best moments of a salon worker's day.
explanation.definitionFit: Highlights are both the standout moments of an event and lightened streaks put into hair at a salon.

clue.text: Scholar head of academy can put in directory

indicators.note: one piece is put in another, so the first letters go inside the directory word

parts.note: a directory is a list of names

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here of academy

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: An academic whose principal can enter them in a directory of staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put in' is the containment signal; 'head of academy' looks like a job title but gives just one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latinist is a scholar specialising in the Latin language and its literature.

clue.text: Stories about soldiers in scene of conflict

indicators.note: stories about soldiers means the story word wraps round the soldiers word

parts.note: ana is a collection of anecdotes or sayings about a person
RE, the Royal Engineers, is a corps of soldiers

explanation.surface: War stories told about soldiers at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals containment; the Royal Engineers are the crossword's usual soldiers, and ana is a collection of anecdotes.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a place where a contest or struggle is fought out, as the arena of war.

clue.text: Strain shown by, say, future head

parts.note: the future is an example of a grammatical tense, hence 'say'
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: A worried thought about the future causes a strained head.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenseness is a state of tension or strain, in the body or in a situation.

clue.text: Scottish dish, good one, consumed by ugly old women

indicators.note: what is consumed by something goes inside it, so the short pieces go into the women word

parts.note: hags are ugly old women
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A good haggis eaten up by a group of old crones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumed by' sets G and I inside HAGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Haggis is the national Scottish pudding of offal, oatmeal and suet cooked in a sheep's stomach.

clue.text: Pops up to get favourable slant from doctor?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to pop in somewhere briefly is to nip in, so pops can mean nips

explanation.surface: Someone appears in order to get a good gloss from a press adviser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns NIPS around. The question mark marks the spin doctor, a political press officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Spin is the favourable gloss a spin doctor, or public-relations adviser, puts on news.

clue.text: Debris Oscar removed from Motown, America

indicators.note: something removed is taken away, so one letter comes out of the city name

parts.note: Motown is a nickname for Detroit, the Motor Town
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
US is short for the United States of America

explanation.surface: An Oscar award is taken out of the Motown debris in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removed' takes the Oscar letter out of the city; Motown is Detroit's nickname, from Motor Town.
explanation.definitionFit: Detritus is loose waste matter or fragments, a synonym for debris.

clue.text: Precedent that's no longer enough?

parts.note: ex means former, no longer current
ample means plenty, enough

explanation.surface: A legal precedent that is now outdated and insufficient.
explanation.definitionFit: An example set earlier serves as a precedent that others may follow.

clue.text: Beneficiary from shelter crossing northern street

indicators.note: the shelter word crosses over, spanning the street word, which sits inside it

parts.note: lee is shelter from the wind
gate is a northern English and Scots word for street, as in York's Stonegate

explanation.surface: An heir collects their legacy from a bus shelter across a street up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' signals the shelter word straddling the street word. Many northern English street names end in -gate, like York's Stonegate.
explanation.definitionFit: A legatee is a person who receives a legacy under a will, a beneficiary.

clue.text: Individual in Greece, one with no future

indicators.note: one piece is in another, so the individual word sits within the country abbreviation

parts.note: GR is the international code for Greece
an individual is one

explanation.surface: A lone man stranded in Greece who has no prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals containment; Greece is shortened to its international vehicle code.
explanation.definitionFit: A goner is someone doomed or past saving, who has no future.

clue.text: Cloisters of church outside a London complex

indicators.note: the church abbreviation stands outside, wrapping round the jumbled letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: complex means intricate, tangled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Church cloisters outside a London building complex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complex' looks like a noun for a group of buildings but is the anagram signal; 'outside' wraps the Church of England round the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonnade is a row of columns; a cloister is a covered walkway lined with them.

clue.text: Developing hospital backed with little money

indicators.note: a word backed is turned back to front

parts.note: san, short for sanatorium, is a hospital
a cent is a small coin, a little money

explanation.surface: A growing hospital funded with very little money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' reverses the short word for sanatorium, a crossword staple for hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nascent is just coming into being and starting to develop.

clue.text: Sadly premature, accepting troop leader's old hearing aid

indicators.note: the jumbled letters accept, taking inside, the letter that leads the troop
sadly can mean badly, in a sorry state, so the letters are rearranged
a word's leader is its first letter, here of troop

explanation.surface: A troop commander's antiquated hearing device, sadly failing too early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' rearranges PREMATURE, and 'accepting' takes in T, the first letter of troop.
explanation.definitionFit: An ear trumpet is a horn-shaped tube once held to the ear to help the deaf hear.

clue.text: Kitchen appliance knocked out of shape

definitions.meaning: a past tense of stave, to break or dent inwards, as in staved in

explanation.surface: A cooker that has been dented.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides a cooker, stove is a past participle of stave, meaning smashed or dented inwards.

clue.text: Moan excessively, to who'll listen, having excess of vegetation?

parts.note: over as a prefix means excessively, as in overdo

indicators.note: words to those who listen are heard, so the moan word counts by its sound

parts.note: to groan is to moan

explanation.surface: Someone complaining too much to anyone who will listen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to who'll listen' is the sound signal, working on the moan word only.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden that is overgrown is covered with too much uncontrolled plant growth.

clue.text: Oval dish — a novel type to begin with

parts.note: She is a novel by H Rider Haggard

indicators.note: to begin with points to the first letter of type

explanation.surface: An oval plate is a new kind of thing at first.
explanation.walkthrough: SHE is H Rider Haggard's adventure novel; then T starts type.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashet is a Scottish and northern English word for a large oval serving plate.

clue.text: Broadcast by possible porter's best friend?

parts.note: a programme broadcast has been aired
porter is a dark beer; ale is the broader name such a beer may go by, hence 'possible'

explanation.surface: A railway porter's loyal companion is broadcast on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'best friend?' alludes to the dog as man's best friend; porter is also a beer, not just a station worker.
explanation.definitionFit: An Airedale is a breed of large terrier, and a dog is proverbially man's best friend.

clue.text: Body of people almost dry up on stage

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter goes

parts.note: an actor corpses by breaking down in laughter, drying up on stage

explanation.surface: A cast who nearly forget their lines in performance.
explanation.walkthrough: To corpse is theatre slang for losing composure; 'almost' drops its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: A corps is an organised body of people, such as a military unit or the corps de ballet.

clue.text: Idiot greeting King Edward's tailor

parts.note: a clot is a fool
hi is a greeting
ER stands for Edwardus Rex, King Edward

explanation.surface: A fool saying hello to a royal outfitter.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothier makes or sells clothes, the trade of a tailor.

clue.text: Sly person losing wife's support

indicators.note: losing means the word gives up a letter

parts.note: a weasel is a sly, crafty person

explanation.surface: A sneaky man loses his wife's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' takes W from WEASEL.
explanation.definitionFit: An easel is a frame that supports a painting or blackboard.

clue.text: More hazardous trail regularly taken by winter sportsperson

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals gives the second and fourth of trail

parts.note: a skier takes part in a winter sport

explanation.surface: A trail used by a skier becomes more dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes RI from trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Riskier means involving greater risk, so more hazardous.

clue.text: Halogen one old woman upset

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, read from bottom to top

parts.note: Enid is a woman's name

explanation.surface: An old woman upset by a chemical element.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses only the woman's name, which reads as an ordinary word for eating once turned.
explanation.definitionFit: Iodine is one of the halogen elements, alongside fluorine, chlorine and bromine.

clue.text: Blunder into rocky peak, provoking panic

indicators.note: one piece goes into another, so the blunder word is placed inside the peak word

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor
to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: A climber's mistake on a rocky summit causes panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' signals containment; a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror is extreme fear, the feeling that grips someone in a panic.

clue.text: Game birds snatching feed in river

indicators.note: the birds snatch the feed word, holding it inside

parts.note: grouse are game birds
to feed is to eat

explanation.surface: Grouse grabbing food by a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snatching' signals the birds holding the feed word; 'Game birds' looks like the definition, but the definition is 'river'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Ouse is a river in eastern England flowing through Bedford, Ely and King's Lynn.

clue.text: Record thus maintained primarily in racecourse

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
so means thus

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter of maintained

explanation.surface: A record kept up mainly at a racetrack.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the first letter of maintained.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs in Surrey is a racecourse, home of the Derby.

clue.text: Tree-dweller father observed crossing railway

indicators.note: the father word spans across the railway abbreviation, holding it inside

parts.note: dad is father

explanation.surface: A dad watched a tree-dwelling creature cross a railway track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' signals the father word spanning the railway abbreviation; 'observed' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A dryad is a tree nymph of Greek myth who lives in a tree.

clue.text: Leader of yobs beheaded bird? That's disgusting!

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here of yobs
a word beheaded loses its first letter

parts.note: a duck is a bird

explanation.surface: A hooligan ringleader decapitates a bird, which is revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' takes D from DUCK, leaving UCK.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuck is an exclamation of disgust.

clue.text: Captain beginning to steam fish

indicators.note: the beginning to a word is its first letter, here of steam

parts.note: a kipper is a smoked herring

explanation.surface: A ship's captain starts to cook a fish by steaming it.
explanation.walkthrough: S starts steam.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipper is the captain of a ship or sports team.

clue.text: Scene of siege currently associated with good fortune

parts.note: luck is good fortune
now means currently

explanation.surface: A place under siege now enjoys some good luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucknow in India was besieged during the 1857 rebellion against British rule.

clue.text: Source of inspiration right behind miners' union's top figure

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so the muse and the right letter follow the union

parts.note: the NUM is the National Union of Mineworkers, the British miners' union
Erato is the Greek muse of love poetry, a source of inspiration

explanation.surface: An inspirational figure stands behind the miners' leader.
explanation.walkthrough: NUM is Britain's National Union of Mineworkers; a muse is the classic source of inspiration.
explanation.definitionFit: In a fraction the numerator is the number written on top of the line.
